definition.title: Accessory dwelling units
definition.handbook_text: Model the effect of allowing one ADU on parcels with existing single-family buildings. Assume detached and semi-detached ADUs of at least 600 square feet are allowed, and no additional parking is required.
definition.description: One ADU of at least 600 sq ft on every lot with a single-family home, with no added parking.

source.citation: Housing Data and Technology Innovation Challenge, Participant Handbook, "Benchmark Policy Scenarios" and "The five scenarios"

notes: Attached single-family lots are included at a much lower physical fit.

parameters.label: Added parking spaces required for an ADU

source.citation: Housing Data and Technology Innovation Challenge, Participant Handbook, "Benchmark Policy Scenarios" and "The five scenarios"

parameters.rationale: The Handbook's ADU scenario requires no additional parking.
parameters.revisit: Only if the Handbook changes.

parameters.label: Share of eligible lots where an ADU is already effectively legal

source.citation: Evidence library entry ev.adu.pew_national_2025: The Pew Charitable Trusts (October 2026), "Accessory Dwelling Units Can Meaningfully Boost Housing Supply", Table 1

parameters.rationale: The default for any state without its own value. Pennsylvania replaces it from its town-rule index (assumptions/calibration/adu_legal_share.yaml); Vermont, whose state law already requires towns to allow ADUs, replaces it from assumptions/calibration/already_legal_vt.yaml. Lots where ADUs are already allowed by right add nothing under the reform. In states without an ADU preemption law, 25 of 196 cities of 100,000 or more (13%) had permissive ADU rules in April 2026, and smaller places tend to be more restrictive, so 10% is the central value. The range runs from 5% to 25%, because a state with a strong preemption law has most lots already legal and needs its own value.
parameters.revisit: For each new state, check whether it has a state ADU law (22 states by August 2026) and set a state value; replace with a town-rule index where one is built.

parameters.label: Share of the appropriation spent on running the program
parameters.rationale: Set aside from the appropriation before any award (staff, outreach, inspection). Judgement range typical of state grant programs that cap administration at about 5-10% of a fund. It is a cost whether or not the rest is used.
parameters.revisit: Set from the bill's administration cap.

parameters.label: State ADU program appropriation, 2027-2031 (lever setting)
parameters.rationale: Benchmark: no program. The variants adu_finance_budget and adu_finance_budget_loan give it the value of adu.budget_appropriation_illustrative.
parameters.revisit: Keep at 0 for the benchmark.

parameters.label: State ADU program appropriation, 2027-2031 (illustrative scenario setting)

source.citation: California Housing Finance Agency, ADU Grant Program: up to $40,000 toward predevelopment and non-recurring closing costs of an ADU (raised from $25,000 in March 2022; funds fully allocated by December 2023)

parameters.rationale: Illustrative scenario setting, not an estimate or a proposal: a one-time appropriation a Pennsylvania committee might test. $20 million at a $25,000 award funds at most 800 awards before administration. California's program shows that a capped fund can be fully allocated within two years. The budget-and-target grid (assumptions/adu_budget_grid.yaml) tries other amounts on the same draws.
parameters.revisit: Set from a bill's appropriation if one is proposed.

parameters.label: Award per funded ADU project (lever setting)
parameters.rationale: Benchmark: no program. The budget variants give it the value of adu.budget_award_amount_illustrative.
parameters.revisit: Keep at 0 for the benchmark.

parameters.label: Award per funded ADU project (illustrative scenario setting)

source.citation: California Housing Finance Agency, ADU Grant Program: up to $40,000 toward predevelopment and non-recurring closing costs of an ADU (raised from $25,000 in March 2022)

parameters.rationale: Illustrative scenario setting: California's first award ceiling. An award never pays more than the owner's own cash share; it replaces owner cash, lowers the break-even rent (more lots pass the rent test) and raises take-up by A(C1) / A(C0), as in the financing lever.
parameters.revisit: Set from a program's term sheet.

parameters.label: Share of eligible would-be builders who apply for and accept an award
parameters.rationale: Not every eligible owner hears of the program or takes on its paperwork, inspection and reporting rules. Judgement range. Awards are handed out first come, first served within each year (pro rata when a year's requests exceed the money left), so owners who would build anyway compete with owners the award brings in.
parameters.revisit: Set from a program's application and acceptance counts.

parameters.label: Share of would-be ADU builders eligible for a program award
parameters.rationale: A state program usually limits awards to owner-occupants under an income limit and to projects that meet its rules. Judgement range: most owners who add an ADU live on the lot; an income limit near the area median leaves out roughly a third to a half of them. The same share applies to owners who would build anyway and to owners the award brings in.
parameters.revisit: Set from a program's eligibility rules and owner income data (ACS tenure by income).

parameters.label: Share of program loan principal never repaid
parameters.rationale: Used only when awards are loans. Home-secured loans to owner-occupants default rarely; a small program with weaker underwriting loses more. Judgement range.
parameters.revisit: Set from a state housing finance agency's second-mortgage loss history.

parameters.label: Share of each award paid as a loan rather than a grant (lever setting)
parameters.rationale: 0 = every award is a grant (no repayment). The variant adu_finance_budget_loan gives it the value of adu.budget_loan_share_loan.
parameters.revisit: A program design choice.

parameters.label: Share of each award paid as a loan (illustrative scenario setting: all loans)
parameters.rationale: Illustrative scenario setting: every award is a loan at adu.financing_program_rate over the loan term, repaid except for the loan loss share.
parameters.revisit: A program design choice.

parameters.label: Smallest program gain that counts as a gain when dividing cost by units
parameters.rationale: A display rule: cost per additional unit is worked out only in draws where the program adds at least half a unit; the other draws are counted as zero-gain draws and their share is reported beside it, never hidden in a ratio.
parameters.revisit: Display rule only.

parameters.label: Yearly rate the state uses to value future loan repayments
parameters.rationale: A loan's net public cost counts the interest the state forgoes: the repaid principal x (1 - present value of the payments at this rate / principal). Near a state's long-term borrowing cost. Judgement range.
parameters.revisit: Use the state's bond yield at the time of the appropriation.

parameters.label: Additional ADU authorizations a program is asked to add in 2027-2031 (illustrative target)
parameters.rationale: Illustrative scenario setting used by the "what would it take" records: awards, award take-up and appropriation needed for this many additional in-window ADU authorizations from the program. The grid in assumptions/adu_budget_grid.yaml tries other targets.
parameters.revisit: Set by the user or a committee's goal.

parameters.label: Yearly return the owner's own cash could earn elsewhere
parameters.rationale: The part of an ADU not paid by a loan is the owner's cash, which could have stayed in savings or investments. Its cost is spread over the loan term like a loan at this rate. Between a savings rate and a stock return.
parameters.revisit: Compare with published savings and Treasury yields when the data pack is rebuilt.

parameters.label: Share of 'by right with conditions' lots where the ADU benchmark changes what an owner may build
parameters.rationale: Where a municipality already allows an ADU by right but only attached, or only with the owner living on the lot, the benchmark (detached or semi-detached, no owner rule) still opens a new option on most lots: the owner who will not live there, or whose lot suits only a detached unit. Some owners would have built the attached form anyway, so not every such lot counts as changed. Used only in counties whose verified rules carry legal-status categories (assumptions/law/hooks.yaml).
parameters.revisit: Count ADU permits by form and owner status in municipalities that dropped owner-occupancy rules.

parameters.label: Share of ADUs not built as a detached building that are made inside the house

source.citation: Terner Center for Housing Innovation, UC Berkeley, statewide survey of California ADU owners (blog summary "What Do ADU Owners Say?")

parameters.rationale: An ADU that is not a separate building is either made inside the house (a basement, attic or garage conversion) or built onto it (an attached addition). Owner surveys report both, in shares of similar size. The split matters for permit statistics: the Building Permits Survey leaves out conversions, and an attached ADU counts only when the permit office classes it as a new attached structure rather than an addition. It does not change the ADU total.
parameters.revisit: Read the survey report's form shares and Pennsylvania ADU permit work-type descriptions.

parameters.label: Share of ADUs on semi-detached or row lots built as detached units
parameters.rationale: Semi-detached and row lots have small rear yards; most ADUs there are semi-detached (attached to the house, over a garage or in a basement). The split sends ADUs to work types carried through the funnel's stages; it does not change the total.
parameters.revisit: Count ADU permits by form on row and twin lots (Philadelphia permit descriptions).

parameters.label: Share of ADUs on detached single-family lots built as detached units

source.citation: Terner Center for Housing Innovation, UC Berkeley, statewide survey of California ADU owners (blog summary "What Do ADU Owners Say?")

parameters.rationale: Owner surveys where both forms are legal find detached units the most common form, with conversions and attached additions the rest. The split sends each kind of lot's ADUs to work types (detached new building, or attached / inside the house) carried through the funnel's stages; it does not change the total. It decides how many ADUs the Building Permits Survey would count (a detached ADU is a new building).
parameters.revisit: Read the survey report's form shares and check them against Pennsylvania permit descriptions.

parameters.label: Share of ADUs that replace a home that would have been built anyway
parameters.rationale: Some ADUs are built by builders who would otherwise have built something else on the lot, or replace legal conversions already counted in the baseline; they are not net new.
parameters.revisit: Estimate from permit data before and after reform in hindcast places.

parameters.label: ADUs approved in Massachusetts in the first year of statewide by-right ADUs

source.citation: Commonwealth of Massachusetts, press release "Governor Healey announces more than 1,200 ADUs approved in first year, with more to come"

parameters.rationale: Cities and towns permitted or approved 1,224 ADUs in 217 communities in the first year after ADUs became allowed by right statewide. A statewide hindcast check on the ramp-up. The state's tracker covers about 84% of the Commonwealth, so this is a floor. Read through a search summary; the page refused a direct download.
parameters.revisit: Read the release and the ADU tracker directly; add later counts.

parameters.label: ADU permits per 100,000 residents in 2025, permissive U.S. cities

source.citation: The Pew Charitable Trusts (October 2026), "Accessory Dwelling Units Can Meaningfully Boost Housing Supply"; ADU permits in 2025 in the 346 most populous U.S. cities, 158 of them with permissive ordinances

parameters.rationale: Cities with permissive ADU rules issued 81 ADU permits per 100,000 residents in 2025, more than 11 times restrictive cities. Heavily shaped by California. Read from the report's published text through a search summary; the page itself refused a direct download.
parameters.revisit: Read the full report and record the table and page.

parameters.label: ADU permits per 100,000 residents in 2025, permissive cities outside California

source.citation: The Pew Charitable Trusts (October 2026), "Accessory Dwelling Units Can Meaningfully Boost Housing Supply"; ADU permits in 2025 in the 346 most populous U.S. cities, 158 of them with permissive ordinances

parameters.rationale: Outside California, cities with permissive rules issued 26 ADU permits per 100,000 residents in 2025. The closer analogue for Pennsylvania; used as a per-capita cross-check on the funnel's result.
parameters.revisit: Read the full report and record the table and page.

parameters.label: ADUs permitted in Seattle in 2023

source.citation: City of Seattle, Office of Planning and Community Development and Department of Construction and Inspections, "2023 Accessory Dwelling Unit Report", page 10

parameters.rationale: 987 ADUs (476 attached, 511 detached) were permitted in 2023, four years after the 2019 reform; the report says permits may be levelling off near 1,000 a year.
parameters.revisit: Add the 2024 report when read.

parameters.label: Average yearly ADUs permitted in Seattle, 2016-2019 (before reform)

source.citation: City of Seattle, Office of Planning and Community Development and Department of Construction and Inspections, "2023 Accessory Dwelling Unit Report", page 10

parameters.rationale: About 263 ADUs a year were permitted from 2016 to 2019, before the reform took effect.
parameters.revisit: None expected; the figure is historical.

parameters.label: Owner cash a state ADU financing program replaces, per ADU (variant)

source.citation: California Housing Finance Agency, ADU Grant Program: up to $40,000 toward predevelopment and non-recurring closing costs of an ADU (raised from $25,000 in March 2022; funds fully allocated by December 2023)

parameters.rationale: A state program that lends or grants part of the owner's cash share. The high end is California's grant ceiling, the central its first ceiling, the low a small predevelopment loan. Never more than the owner's own cash.
parameters.revisit: Set from the terms of a Pennsylvania program if one is proposed.

parameters.label: Share of the expected ADU rent a lender counts toward a larger loan (variant)

source.citation: Fannie Mae Selling Guide B3-3.8-01, Rental Income: rental income from one ADU on a one-unit principal residence may be used to qualify (purchase or limited cash-out refinance), limited to 30% of total qualifying income

parameters.rationale: A Fannie Mae-style rule lets a lender count part of an ADU's rent as income. The rule is written for homes that already have an ADU; the access case assumes a renovation or home-equity lender treats a planned ADU the same way. After the usual vacancy factor and the 30%-of-income cap, a judgement share of the expected rent supports an added loan payment: the added loan is share x rent / loan payment per dollar, never more than the owner's remaining cash. Range 0.05-0.35, central 0.2: below Fannie Mae's 75% of gross rent because the 30%-of-income cap and the lender's debt-to-income limit bind first, and the rule is not yet written for a planned ADU. (A first draft of 0.1-0.5 let the counted rent alone cover all of the owner's cash on Testland, which overstates what a lender would accept.)
parameters.revisit: Check renovation-loan rules for future ADU rent and lender practice in Pennsylvania.

parameters.label: Share of ADU cost an owner can borrow, easy financing (variant)
parameters.rationale: Renovation mortgages that count future ADU rent as income let an owner borrow nearly all of the cost. Used only by the variant 'adu_financing_easy'.
parameters.revisit: Check against secondary-market rules for rental income from an ADU.

parameters.label: ADU loan rate above the 30-year mortgage rate, easy financing (variant)
parameters.rationale: A cash-out refinance or renovation first mortgage prices close to the 30-year rate. Used only by the variant 'adu_financing_easy'.
parameters.revisit: Compare renovation-mortgage rates with the 30-year rate.

parameters.label: Owner cash a state ADU financing program replaces, per ADU (lever setting)
parameters.rationale: Benchmark: no program. The variants adu_financing_access and adu_both give it the range of adu.financing_access_program_amount.
parameters.revisit: Keep at 0 for the benchmark.

parameters.label: Yearly interest rate on program money (0 = grant or forgivable loan)
parameters.rationale: State homeowner programs lend below market or forgive the loan. An owner uses program money only where it costs no more per dollar than their own cash (adu.cash_return), so the program never raises the monthly cost.
parameters.revisit: Set from a program's term sheet.

parameters.label: Share of the expected ADU rent a lender counts toward a larger loan (lever setting)
parameters.rationale: Benchmark: lenders size a loan for a new ADU without its future rent. The variants adu_financing_access and adu_both give it the range of adu.financing_access_rent_income_share.
parameters.revisit: Keep at 0 for the benchmark.

parameters.label: Share of ADU cost an owner can borrow, tight financing (variant)
parameters.rationale: Tighter home-equity lending (lower combined loan-to-value limits) leaves the owner to pay more in cash. Used only by the variant 'adu_financing_tight'.
parameters.revisit: Set from the Federal Reserve senior loan officer survey and lender home-equity limits.

parameters.label: Home-equity rate above the 30-year mortgage rate, tight financing (variant)
parameters.rationale: Home-equity lines price off the prime rate and widen when lenders tighten; a construction or renovation loan for an ADU costs more than a first mortgage. Used only by the variant 'adu_financing_tight'.
parameters.revisit: Compare published home-equity line rates with the 30-year rate over 2024-2026.

parameters.label: Position inside the calibrated ADU fit range
parameters.rationale: The physical-fit share comes from the calibration table assumptions/calibration/adu_fit.yaml, which gives a central, low and high share for each building type and area type. Each draw picks one position: -1 puts every cell at its low, 0 at its central value, +1 at its high. All cells move together, so errors do not cancel across tracts.
parameters.revisit: Replace by the fit-transfer error band once the physical-fit transfer model (with leave-one-county-out error) is run.

parameters.label: Share of semi-detached and row lots with room for the ADU
parameters.rationale: Measured between about 0.02 (rows) and 0.29 (semi-detached) in two cities; attached lots rarely have the yard space.
parameters.revisit: Becomes calibrated from the physical-fit table.

parameters.label: Share of single-family detached lots with room for the ADU
parameters.rationale: Measured near 0.54 for detached homes in two Pennsylvania cities with 4-foot setbacks. Suburban and rural lots are larger, so the high end is well above the city value.
parameters.revisit: Becomes calibrated from the physical-fit table.

parameters.label: Construction cost of a new detached ADU per square foot
parameters.rationale: No free public survey of ADU costs in Pennsylvania was found. Published owner surveys from California report medians near $250 per square foot; the range is wide and skewed up for small-unit cost premiums and 2026 prices.
parameters.revisit: Look for a free public cost source (state housing agency, census construction cost data, or a Pennsylvania builder survey).

parameters.label: Smallest lever effect, as a share of the benchmark, that counts as binding
parameters.rationale: The lever card names timing or financing as the binding factor when its P50 effect is at least this share of the benchmark's P50 added units; when neither lever reaches it, eligibility (who gains a legal right to build and has room) is named. A display rule only.
parameters.revisit: Raise it if small effects are read as large.

parameters.label: ADU lever runs use the yearly hazard on surviving eligible sites (method switch, 0 = off)
parameters.rationale: Benchmark: the funnel's linear take-up (feasible lots x yearly take-up x sum of the ramp, capped at the feasible lots), unchanged. The hazard variants give it the value of adu.lever_hazard_method_on.
parameters.revisit: Keep at 0 for the benchmark.

parameters.label: ADU lever runs use the yearly hazard on surviving eligible sites (variant: on)
parameters.rationale: Method setting, not an estimate. Each year a share of the eligible sites still without an ADU application files one (projects = remaining sites x hazard), the sites left fall, and applications reach a permit after the application-to-permit lag, so projects not finished by 2031 pass the window. The yearly hazard is the funnel's take-up x ramp, scaled once so that, with no depletion and today's lag, permits in 2027-2031 equal the benchmark's (the take-up evidence is counted in permits).
parameters.revisit: A method switch; revisit only if the benchmark itself moves to the hazard.

parameters.label: ADU loan rate above the 30-year mortgage rate
parameters.rationale: Home-equity and construction loans usually cost somewhat more than a first mortgage.
parameters.revisit: Source a published home-equity rate series.

parameters.label: Share of ADU cost financed with a loan
parameters.rationale: Most owners borrow part of the cost (in Seattle about 62% used a loan for some of it); some pay cash.
parameters.revisit: Cite owner survey results once read from the primary reports.

parameters.label: Loan term for ADU financing
parameters.rationale: Home-equity lines run about 20 years; construction-to-permanent loans up to 30.
parameters.revisit: Check typical home-equity and renovation loan terms.

parameters.label: Correction from the census building count to real lots
parameters.rationale: Counting lots from census units-in-structure tables overstates real lots by about 9-13% in two cities where both were measured; this scales it down.
parameters.revisit: Recompute from Tier 2 parcel counties.

parameters.label: Massachusetts: Boston's share of Suffolk County single-family lots (used only without a tract-to-town table)
parameters.rationale: Chapter 40A does not cover Boston. Suffolk County is Boston, Chelsea, Revere and Winthrop; Boston holds most of its homes, while Revere and Winthrop hold more than their share of single-family houses. Used for every Suffolk tract only when the pack has no tract_municipalities table; with the table, each tract's measured Boston share of 2020 housing units is used instead. The Massachusetts pack carries the table since 2026-11-26 (tract-crosswalk step), so this range is now only the fallback for a pack built without that step. Used only by the named variant ma_adu_state_floor.
parameters.revisit: Drop once every way of building the Massachusetts pack writes tract_municipalities (the tract-crosswalk step can fail and be skipped).

parameters.label: Massachusetts: share of homes under the size floor where the town already allows a 600 sq ft ADU
parameters.rationale: A town may allow more than the state floor; some bylaws allow a fixed size (for example 900 sq ft) whatever the house. On those lots the benchmark's 600 sq ft adds no new right. Team judgement; local bylaws were not read. Used only by the named variant ma_adu_state_floor.
parameters.revisit: Read the ADU size rule of a sample of Massachusetts bylaws.

parameters.label: Massachusetts: share of single-family primary dwellings under 1,200 sq ft
parameters.rationale: Under c. 40A § 1A an ADU may be capped at half the principal dwelling's gross floor area, so a 600 sq ft ADU is protected only where the house has at least 1,200 sq ft. The pack has no floor-area data (the ACS tables it reads count structures, not square feet); this is team judgement for the share of single-family homes below 1,200 sq ft, wide on purpose. The 1,200 sq ft line follows from the statute and the benchmark size and is checked in assumptions/law/statutory_rights.yaml. Used only by the named variant ma_adu_state_floor.
parameters.revisit: Replace with assessor floor areas (statewide parcel data) or the AHS floor-area distribution for Massachusetts.

parameters.label: Massachusetts: share of single-family lots inside a single-family residential zoning district
parameters.rationale: M.G.L. c. 40A § 3 protects one ADU by right only in a single-family residential zoning district. Most single-family homes stand in such districts; older cities also zone many of them two-family or mixed, where the state right does not reach. Not measured: no statewide zoning map in the pack. Used only by the named variant ma_adu_state_floor.
parameters.revisit: Replace with a lot count from a statewide zoning-district map when one can be read by script.

parameters.label: Massachusetts: share of lots beyond the station distance where the town requires the one ADU parking space
parameters.rationale: Section 3 lets a town require at most one added parking space for an ADU, and none within 0.5 miles of a listed station. Whether a town uses that allowance is in its bylaw, which was not read. Team judgement, wide on purpose. Used only by the named variant ma_adu_state_floor.
parameters.revisit: Read the ADU parking rule of a sample of Massachusetts bylaws.

parameters.label: Smallest ADU the benchmark allows

source.citation: Housing Data and Technology Innovation Challenge, Participant Handbook, "Benchmark Policy Scenarios" and "The five scenarios"

parameters.rationale: The Handbook assumes detached and semi-detached ADUs of at least 600 square feet are allowed.
parameters.revisit: Only if the Handbook changes.

parameters.label: Rent premium of a new unit over the census median
parameters.rationale: Census medians include long-time tenants with older, cheaper leases, so a newly built unit usually rents above them.
parameters.revisit: Compare with HUD Fair Market Rents for recent movers.

parameters.label: Share of fitting lots where an owner builds for family use regardless of rent
parameters.rationale: Some ADUs house relatives or the owners themselves, so they are built even where rent would not cover cost. This is added to the financially feasible share.
parameters.revisit: Cite owner survey shares of family use (Oregon, California).

parameters.label: Vacancy, upkeep, insurance and property tax as a share of rent
parameters.rationale: A common rule of thumb for small rentals is that 25-35% of gross rent goes to running costs.
parameters.revisit: Build from parts: rental vacancy, property tax rate, insurance, upkeep.

parameters.label: Owner cash at which half of would-be ADU builders can pay their share
parameters.rationale: Used only as a ratio, so the benchmark is unchanged: when a lever lowers the owner's cash need from C0 to C1, take-up rises by A(C1) / A(C0) with A(C) = 1 / (1 + (C / median)^shape), the share of owners whose savings or equity cover C. Today's take-up already reflects today's cash need.
parameters.revisit: Set from the Survey of Consumer Finances: homeowners' liquid assets and home equity lines.

parameters.label: Steepness of owners' ability to pay cash for an ADU
parameters.rationale: The log-logistic shape in A(C) = 1 / (1 + (C / median)^shape). Higher means owners' cash is bunched near the median, so a program that crosses it matters more.
parameters.revisit: Fit with adu.owner_cash_capacity_median.

parameters.label: Building and zoning permit fees for one ADU
parameters.rationale: Permit fees for a small unit are usually a small fixed fee plus a share of construction value.
parameters.revisit: Sample published fee schedules of Pennsylvania municipalities.

parameters.label: Spread of ADU application-to-permit days, today (log standard deviation)
parameters.rationale: The lag is drawn as a lognormal: P90 / P50 = exp(1.2816 x spread) and P75 / P50 = exp(0.6745 x spread). Central: Philadelphia's one-unit stage lag, P90 491 / P50 141 days, gives ln(3.48) / 1.2816 = 0.97 (all new homes 533 / 160 give 0.94). Low and high: the California ADU donor ranges, P75 / median 973 / 670 gives 0.55 and 591 / 196 gives 1.63. Illustrative/transferred.
parameters.revisit: Fit to a Pennsylvania cohort with application dates and right-censored pending cases.

parameters.label: Median days from ADU application to building permit, today (illustrative/transferred)

source.citation: City of Philadelphia, Department of Licenses and Inspections, building and zoning permits; zoning-issued to building-issued stage lag, one-unit new homes (assumptions/calibration/permit_lag_phl.yaml, stage_lag_issued.new_1.all)

California HCD Housing Element Annual Progress Report, Table A and A2; ADU application-to-permit median days across California and three cities (assumptions/calibration/apr_timing_donor_ca.yaml, ranges.adu.application_to_permit)

parameters.rationale: No Pennsylvania permit table publishes an application date, so this lag is illustrative. Low: Philadelphia's observed zoning-to-building stage median for one-unit new homes (141 days), a floor because it leaves out zoning review. High: the slowest California ADU application-to-permit median in the donor file (670 days). Central: between the fastest California median (196 days) and Philadelphia's stage lag plus a zoning review. The engine checks the range against both calibration files on every run (adu_levers.lag_anchors).
parameters.revisit: Replace with a Pennsylvania application-to-issue lag once any municipality publishes application dates.

parameters.label: First-year ADU permits as a share of the steady yearly rate
parameters.rationale: Permits climb for a few years after a reform; Seattle's first full year was about half its later plateau.
parameters.revisit: Fit to published post-reform permit paths (the planned hindcasts).

parameters.label: Years for ADU permits to reach the steady yearly rate
parameters.rationale: Seattle reached its plateau about three years after its 2019 reform.
parameters.revisit: Fit to published post-reform permit paths (the planned hindcasts).

parameters.label: One-bedroom rent as a share of the all-unit median rent

source.citation: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2020-2024 5-year estimates, table B25031 (median gross rent by bedrooms), table-based summary file, county rows for Pennsylvania (67 counties)

parameters.rationale: A 600 sq ft ADU rents like a one-bedroom. Tract one-bedroom rents are often blank or noisy, so the tract's median rent is scaled by its county's ratio of one-bedroom to all-unit median rent. Across Pennsylvania's 67 counties the median ratio is 0.77, with the 10th to 90th percentile 0.70 to 0.86. Where a county ratio is available the engine uses it; this entry is the fallback and its range.
parameters.revisit: Recompute when a new ACS 5-year release is fetched.

parameters.label: Net rent needed per dollar of annual cost to build
parameters.rationale: An owner builds for rent when net rent covers the yearly cost of the loan (and the return the cash could earn elsewhere). 1.0 is break-even.
parameters.revisit: Calibrate jointly with take-up (the planned ADU take-up fit).

parameters.label: Site work and utility runs for one ADU
parameters.rationale: Trenching, sewer and water lines and electrical service; the high end covers septic upgrades where there is no public sewer.
parameters.revisit: Source from public ADU cost guides; split sewered and septic lots.

parameters.label: Full installed site and utility cost for one ADU (variant: full installed cost)
parameters.rationale: The benchmark line (adu.site_utility_cost) covers trenching and service runs. The full installed case adds what an owner meets on many lots: a new electric service or panel upgrade, separate water and sewer laterals or meters, and on unsewered lots a septic upgrade. Used only by the variant 'adu_full_installed_cost'.
parameters.revisit: Price from published ADU cost guides and utility service-upgrade fee schedules.

parameters.label: Design, permit preparation and contingency as a share of construction (fees not included)
parameters.rationale: Design, permit work and contingency typically add a fifth to construction cost on small projects.
parameters.revisit: Source from public ADU cost guides or owner surveys.

parameters.label: Years after January 1, 2027 before ADU permits start to respond
parameters.rationale: The benchmark reform is assumed to be in force on the first day of the window (baseline.first_year). The slow start of permits is carried by the ramp (adu.ramp_first_year_share), not by a delay. Set above 0 to model a later effective date or a local adoption deadline.
parameters.revisit: Set from a bill's effective date when a bill, not the benchmark, is modelled.

parameters.label: Share of feasible lots that add an ADU each year

source.citation: Evidence library entry ev.adu.seattle_2019: City of Seattle, "2024 ADU Annual Report", Exhibit 2 (ADUs permitted since 2005)
Evidence library entry ev.adu.massachusetts_2025: Commonwealth of Massachusetts, "Accessory Dwelling Unit Tracker" and first-year press release
Evidence library entry ev.adu.california_apr: California HCD, Housing Element Annual Progress Report data, Table A2 (ADU permits by year)
Evidence library entry ev.adu.pew_national_2025: The Pew Charitable Trusts (October 2026), "Accessory Dwelling Units Can Meaningfully Boost Housing Supply"

parameters.rationale: The main behavioural parameter. About 1% a year of lots where an ADU fits and pays is consistent with the order of magnitude seen after reform: Seattle's permits rose to about 3.5 times the pre-reform rate (about 910 a year in 2022-2024), Massachusetts approved 1,224 ADUs in its first by-right year and 2,084 in eighteen months, and permissive cities outside California issued 26 permits per 100,000 residents in 2025. None of these is measured per feasible lot, so the range is not narrowed until the planned ADU take-up fit sets it.
parameters.revisit: Becomes calibrated by the planned ADU take-up fit on jurisdictions with published ADU permits (the California Table A2 panel, Seattle, Massachusetts); check against the per-capita rates below.

parameters.label: Share of the slow tail of approval times pulled to the median, predictable approval (variant)
parameters.rationale: A predictable-approval rule (a review clock with deemed approval, or pre-approved ADU plans) mainly shortens the slow cases: every lag above the median moves this share of the way to the median, so P75-P90 fall and the median stays. Half is a middle judgement; a quarter is a weak clock, three quarters a strict one with pre-approved plans. Applicants and the chance of being issued stay the same (timing only).
parameters.revisit: Set from a jurisdiction's lag distribution before and after a review clock or pre-approved plans.

parameters.label: Years after 2031 the ADU lag model keeps simulating
parameters.rationale: Projects whose permits come after 2031 stay in the simulation so that movement into the window is traceable. Ten more years let nearly every application filed in 2027-2031 reach its permit; those still waiting at the end are reported as pending (right-censored), never dropped.
parameters.revisit: Only a display and accounting setting.

parameters.label: Share of the slow tail of approval times pulled to the median (lever setting)
parameters.rationale: Benchmark: approval times as today (no pull). The variants adu_timing_reliable and adu_both give it the range of adu.timing_reliable_tail_pull_share.
parameters.revisit: Keep at 0 for the benchmark.

parameters.label: Floor area of the modelled ADU
parameters.rationale: The pro forma prices a unit at the benchmark minimum, with some owners building larger. The same size is used in every ADU scenario so that differences between scenarios come from eligibility, not size.
parameters.revisit: Check against size data in published ADU permit reports.

parameters.label: ADUs allowed per lot

source.citation: Housing Data and Technology Innovation Challenge, Participant Handbook, "Benchmark Policy Scenarios" and "The five scenarios"

parameters.rationale: The Handbook's ADU scenario allows one ADU on parcels with an existing single-family building.
parameters.revisit: Only if the Handbook changes.

parameters.label: Water and sewer connection fees for one ADU
parameters.rationale: Tap fees vary widely by authority; large cities charge a few hundred dollars, many suburban authorities several thousand. SB 1346 sets this to 0.
parameters.revisit: Sample published tap-fee schedules of Pennsylvania authorities.

parameters.label: Utility connection fees for an ADU with its own meters (variant: full installed cost)
parameters.rationale: Where an authority treats an ADU with its own meter as a new connection, the tap and capacity fees are those of a new home. Used only by the variant 'adu_full_installed_cost'.
parameters.revisit: Sample published tap-fee schedules of Pennsylvania water and sewer authorities.

parameters.label: Value an ADU adds, as a share of the host home's value
parameters.rationale: Used only for a value-based feasibility test: an ADU pays where the value it adds (this share of the home's value) covers its total cost. Appraisal practice credits a second unit with a fifth to a third of the main home's value; the range is wide.
parameters.revisit: Source from appraisal studies or sales of homes with and without ADUs.

parameters.label: First calendar year counted
parameters.rationale: Reforms are assumed to take effect on January 1, 2027, so the five years counted are 2027-2031.
parameters.revisit: Change only if the assumed effective date changes.

parameters.label: Years in the projection horizon

source.citation: Housing Data and Technology Innovation Challenge, Participant Handbook, "Benchmark Policy Scenarios" and "The five scenarios"

parameters.rationale: The Handbook asks every team to assume a five-year horizon.
parameters.revisit: Only if the Handbook changes.

parameters.label: 30-year fixed mortgage rate

source.citation: Freddie Mac, Primary Mortgage Market Survey, weekly history file, 30-year fixed rate (2026 weeks through Nov 19, 2026)

parameters.rationale: The 2026 average of the weekly 30-year rate was 6.56%, with weeks between 5.98% and 7.40%; the latest week (Nov 19, 2026) was 7.28%. The range is a little wider than 2026's because the horizon runs to 2031.
parameters.revisit: Refresh from the PMMS file when the data pack is rebuilt.

parameters.label: Number of assumptions named in the "what would narrow the range" research agenda
parameters.rationale: The agenda names the few assumptions whose first-order share of the output's variance is largest. Three keeps it short enough to act on.
parameters.revisit: Revisit if a reform has more than three inputs of similar weight.

parameters.label: Homes added (state, five years) for the first "chance of adding at least" readout
parameters.rationale: A reform that clears this bar does something visible in at least a few places; below it the gain is lost in the noise of statewide permit counts.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with the spread of reform results once all five reforms are final.

parameters.label: Homes added (state, five years) for the second "chance of adding at least" readout
parameters.rationale: About two hundred homes a year statewide: a gain a state housing agency would notice in its annual permit totals.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with the spread of reform results once all five reforms are final.

parameters.label: Homes added (state, five years) for the third "chance of adding at least" readout
parameters.rationale: About one thousand homes a year statewide: a gain of the size the largest benchmark reforms reach in their middle estimates.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with the spread of reform results once all five reforms are final.

parameters.label: Homes added (state, five years) for the fourth "chance of adding at least" readout
parameters.rationale: About two thousand homes a year statewide: a gain that would change a state's housing outlook, a high bar for any single reform.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with the spread of reform results once all five reforms are final.

parameters.label: Width ratio (added homes to baseline) under which the effect is called "much less" uncertain than the level
parameters.rationale: When the likely range (P90 minus P10) of a reform's added homes is under a quarter of the width of the baseline's likely range, the sentence says the reform's effect is "much less" uncertain than the future level of building; under one it says "less"; otherwise it says the two are about as uncertain.
parameters.revisit: Revisit if readers misread the sentence in user testing.

parameters.label: Homes added in a tract (middle estimate) where the second tract-column class starts
parameters.rationale: Below one home over five years a tract's gain is in the first class, "under one home": the reform reaches the tract, but barely. Each break is five times the one before, so the classes stay readable from a single ADU to a block of apartments.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with the statewide distribution of tract gains once the map is in use.

parameters.label: Homes added in a tract (middle estimate) where the third tract-column class starts
parameters.rationale: About one home a year in one tract. Most tracts gain between one and five homes under a single reform, so this break marks the tracts that gain clearly more.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with the statewide distribution of tract gains once the map is in use.

parameters.label: Homes added in a tract (middle estimate) where the top tract-column class starts
parameters.rationale: About five homes a year in one tract: a gain a neighbourhood would notice, mostly near major transit stops or in large tracts with many single-family lots.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with the statewide distribution of tract gains once the map is in use.

parameters.label: Smallest middle-estimate gain that earns the verdict "Adds a lot"
parameters.rationale: A reform whose middle estimate (P50) adds at least this share of the baseline's five-year permits is called "Adds a lot". One home in twenty is large next to the year-to-year swing in statewide permits.
parameters.revisit: Revisit once the benchmark reforms are compared with observed reforms.

parameters.label: Smallest middle-estimate gain that earns the verdict "Adds some"
parameters.rationale: Below this share of the baseline's five-year permits (middle estimate, P50) a reform is called "Little effect": the gain is smaller than the rounding in most published permit totals.
parameters.revisit: Revisit once the benchmark reforms are compared with observed reforms.

parameters.label: Cost of one surface parking space, land and construction

source.citation: Victoria Transport Policy Institute, Transportation Cost and Benefit Analysis II, chapter 5.4 "Parking Costs" (version of 3 October 2022), Table 5.4.4-1

parameters.rationale: The review's summary table puts surface parking land and construction at about $8,000 per space in 2022 dollars. Low covers cheap rural land; high covers urban land.
parameters.revisit: Update the price year to 2026 and check against a Pennsylvania cost estimate.

parameters.label: Equal-count bins used to estimate each input's share of the output's variance
parameters.rationale: The draws are sorted by one input and cut into this many bins with the same number of draws each. Ten bins of two hundred draws each keep the variance inside every bin well measured while still following a curved link.
parameters.revisit: Revisit if the number of draws changes a lot.

variants.name: adu_financing_tight
variants.title: ADUs with tight homeowner financing
variants.question: How many fewer ADUs if owners can borrow less, at a higher rate?

variants.name: adu_financing_easy
variants.title: ADUs with easy homeowner financing
variants.question: How many more ADUs if owners can borrow nearly all of the cost near the mortgage rate?

variants.name: adu_full_installed_cost
variants.title: ADUs at full installed cost (own meters, service upgrades)
variants.question: What if every ADU needs a new electric service, its own utility laterals and new-home tap fees?

variants.name: adu_timing_reliable
variants.title: ADUs with predictable approval (slow reviews pulled to the median)
variants.question: If the slowest ADU reviews got faster, how many permits move into 2027-2031? Same applicants, same chance of a permit (timing only; lag illustrative/transferred).

variants.name: adu_financing_access
variants.title: ADUs with homeowner financing access (state program + counted rent)
variants.question: If a state program pays part of the owner's cash share and lenders count part of the ADU's rent, how many more ADUs become feasible?

variants.name: adu_both
variants.title: ADUs with predictable approval and financing access
variants.question: With both levers on the same draws: how many authorizations move into 2027-2031, and how many are newly feasible?

variants.name: adu_hazard_reference
variants.title: ADU benchmark worked out with the hazard on surviving sites (method check)
variants.question: How much does the benchmark move when take-up uses up a finite stock of eligible sites and permits follow applications after a lag? (A disclosed method sensitivity; the benchmark headline is unchanged.)

variants.name: adu_timing_conserved
variants.title: ADUs with predictable approval, projects conserved over an extended horizon
variants.question: If the slowest ADU reviews got faster, how many permits move into 2027-2031, and do all projects still show up once later years are counted? (Timing only; lag illustrative/transferred.)

variants.name: adu_finance_budget
variants.title: ADUs with a budget-capped state grant program (illustrative $20 million, $25,000 awards)
variants.question: With a fixed appropriation, how many owners are served, how many additional ADUs are authorized in 2027-2031 beyond those who would build anyway, and at what net public cost?

variants.name: adu_finance_budget_loan
variants.title: ADUs with a budget-capped state loan program (illustrative $20 million, $25,000 loans)
variants.question: The same capped program paid as loans: how many additional ADUs, and what is the net public cost once repayments and losses are counted?

variants.name: ma_adu_state_floor
variants.title: ADUs in Massachusetts: only the right the benchmark adds to the state ADU law
variants.question: If the already-legal share comes from the state ADU law itself (c. 40A § 1A size cap of half the house or 900 sq ft, § 3 parking rule near listed stations, single-family districts, Boston outside chapter 40A), tract by tract, instead of the labelled statewide range, how many ADUs does the benchmark add? Only lots where the benchmark gives a right the state law does not count.

variants.name: adu_zoning_districts
variants.title: ADUs with the zoning-district reading in the sample (Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Frankstown)
variants.question: If, in the three sample jurisdictions, the already-legal share comes from their zoning districts (verified code text only: known by right, conditions relaxed, newly eligible, discretionary, unresolved at the statewide range) instead of the benchmark's share, how many ADUs does the benchmark add?

variants.name: adu_zoning_districts_guidance
variants.title: ADUs with the zoning-district reading, counting Philadelphia's 2022 ADU checklist (guidance, a sensitivity)
variants.question: The same zoning-district reading, but also counting the City of Philadelphia's own ADU checklist (guidance, not the code): how many ADUs does the benchmark add?

variants.name: adu_capacity_screen
variants.title: ADUs screened for practical capacity (sewer, flood zone, steep slope)
variants.question: How many of the ADUs can be built in practice once lots without public sewer, lots in the flood zone and steep lots are screened?
